'''''Cannabis sativa''''' is an annual [[Herbaceous plant|herbaceous]] [[flowering plant]]. The species was first classified by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1753.<ref>Greg Green, ''The Cannabis Breeder's Bible'', Green Candy Press, 2005, pp. 15-16 {{ISBN|9781931160278}}</ref> The specific epithet ''[[Sativum|sativa]]'' means 'cultivated'. Indigenous to [[East Asia|Eastern Asia]], the plant is now of [[cosmopolitan distribution]] due to widespread cultivation.<ref name="FlorianKronkright1991">{{cite book| vauthors = Florian ML, Kronkright DP, Norton RE |title=The Conservation of Artifacts Made from Plant Materials|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Vp5OAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA49|date=21 March 1991|publisher=Getty Publications|isbn=978-0-89236-160-1|pages=49–}}</ref> It has been cultivated throughout [[recorded history]] and used as a source of [[Hemp#fibre|industrial fiber]], [[Hemp oil|seed oil]], [[Hempnut|food]], and [[Medical cannabis|medicine]]. It is also used as [[Cannabis (drug)|a recreational drug]] and for [[entheogenic use of cannabis|religious and spiritual purposes]].

In 2011, a whole sequenced genome of the species has been published.<ref>DOI 10.1186/gb-2011-12-10-r102</ref>

==Description==
{{Main|Cannabis|Cannabis cultivation}}
[[File:Cannabis Sativa tree.jpg|thumb|242x242px|A female sativa cannabis strain in flowering or "budding" stage]]
The flowers of ''Cannabis sativa'' plants are most often either male or female, but only plants displaying female pistils can be or turn hermaphrodite. Males can never become hermaphrodites.<ref name="SHARMA2011">{{cite book| vauthors = Sharma OP |title= Plant Taxonomy | edition = 2nd |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Roi0lwSXFnUC&pg=PA459|year=2011|publisher=Tata McGraw-Hill Education|isbn=978-1-259-08137-8|pages=459–}}</ref> It is a short-day flowering plant, with staminate (male) plants usually taller and less robust than pistillate (female or male) plants.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=200006342 |title=Cannabis sativa in Flora of North America @ efloras.org |access-date=2017-05-21 |archive-date=2017-03-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170303042937/http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=200006342 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=The Difference Between Male and Female Cannabis Plants |url=https://unitedcannabisseeds.com/the-complete-cannabis-sexing-guide/ |publisher=United Cannabis Seeds |access-date=22 March 2021 |archive-date=5 December 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221205115948/https://unitedcannabisseeds.com/the-complete-cannabis-sexing-guide/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> The [[flower]]s of the female plant are arranged in [[raceme]]s and can produce hundreds of seeds. Male plants shed their pollen and die several weeks prior to seed ripening on the female plants. Under typical conditions with a light period of 12 to 14 hours, both sexes are produced in equal numbers because of heritable [[XY sex-determination system|X and Y chromosomes]].<ref name="ClarkeMerlin2013">{{cite book|vauthors=Clarke R, Merlin M|title=Cannabis: Evolution and Ethnobotany|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=poenY6QMq8UC&pg=PA16|date=1 September 2013|publisher=University of California Press|isbn=978-0-520-95457-1|pages=16–|access-date=27 February 2018|archive-date=20 April 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230420161333/https://books.google.com/books?id=poenY6QMq8UC&pg=PA16|url-status=live}}</ref> Although genetic factors dispose a plant to become male or female, environmental factors including the [[Diurnal cycle|diurnal light cycle]] can alter sexual expression.<ref>{{Cite journal|vauthors=Schaffner JH|date=1921-01-01|title=Influence of Environment on Sexual Expression in Hemp|journal=Botanical Gazette|volume=71|issue=3|pages=197–219|doi=10.1086/332818|jstor=2469863|s2cid=85156955|url=https://zenodo.org/record/1431411|access-date=2019-07-03|archive-date=2020-07-27|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200727073708/https://zenodo.org/record/1431411|url-status=live}}</ref> Naturally occurring [[monoecious]] plants, with both male and female parts, are either sterile or fertile;{{clarify|reason="Either sterile or fertile" is a tautology. Like "either alive or dead".|date=March 2022}} but artificially induced "[[hermaphrodites]]" can have fully functional reproductive organs.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Marijuana plant anatomy and life cycles |url=https://www.leafly.com/learn/growing/marijuana-plant-anatomy |access-date=2023-02-24 |website=Leafly |language=en-US |archive-date=2023-02-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230224014134/https://www.leafly.com/learn/growing/marijuana-plant-anatomy |url-status=live }}</ref> "Feminized" seed sold by many commercial seed suppliers<ref>{{Cite web |title="Feminized Seeds." Hypno Seeds |url=https://hypnoseeds.com/feminized-seeds/ |access-date= |website=}}</ref> are derived from artificially "hermaphroditic" females that lack the male gene, or by treating the plants with hormones or silver [[thiosulfate]].

=== Chemical constituents ===
{{Main|Cannabis (drug)}}
[[File:Tetrahydrocannabinol.svg|thumb|right|200px|Δ<sup>9</sup>-[[tetrahydrocannabinol]] (THC)]]
[[File:Cannabis sativa Koehler drawing.jpg|thumb|right|''Cannabis sativa'', scientific drawing from c. 1900]]

Although the main [[psychoactive]] constituent of ''Cannabis'' is [[tetrahydrocannabinol]] (THC), the plant is known to contain more than 500 compounds, among them at least 113 [[cannabinoid]]s; however, most of these "minor" cannabinoids are only produced in trace amounts.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Aizpurua-Olaizola O, Soydaner U, Öztürk E, Schibano D, Simsir Y, Navarro P, Etxebarria N, Usobiaga A | display-authors = 6 | title = Evolution of the Cannabinoid and Terpene Content during the Growth of Cannabis sativa Plants from Different Chemotypes | language = EN | journal = Journal of Natural Products | volume = 79 | issue = 2 | pages = 324–31 | date = February 2016 | pmid = 26836472 | doi = 10.1021/acs.jnatprod.5b00949 | bibcode = 2016JNAtP..79..324A | hdl = 1874/350973 | url = https://figshare.com/articles/journal_contribution/5028338 | access-date = 2022-11-18 | archive-date = 2023-01-05 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20230105025827/https://figshare.com/articles/journal_contribution/Evolution_of_the_Cannabinoid_and_Terpene_Content_during_the_Growth_of_Cannabis_sativa_Plants_from_Different_Chemotypes/5028338 | url-status = live }}</ref> Besides THC, another cannabinoid produced in high concentrations by some plants is [[cannabidiol]] (CBD), which is not psychoactive but has recently been shown to block the effect of THC in the nervous system.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Russo EB | title = Taming THC: potential cannabis synergy and phytocannabinoid-terpenoid entourage effects | journal = British Journal of Pharmacology | volume = 163 | issue = 7 | pages = 1344–64 | date = August 2011 | pmid = 21749363 | pmc = 3165946 | doi = 10.1111/j.1476-5381.2011.01238.x }}</ref> Differences in the chemical composition of ''Cannabis'' varieties may produce different effects in humans. Synthetic THC, called [[dronabinol]], does not contain cannabidiol (CBD), [[cannabinol]] (CBN), or other cannabinoids, which is one reason why its [[Pharmacology|pharmacological]] effects may differ significantly from those of natural ''Cannabis'' preparations.

Beside cannabinoids, the chemical constituents of ''Cannabis'' include about 120 compounds responsible for its [[Cannabis flower essential oil|characteristic aroma]]. These are mainly volatile [[terpene]]s and [[sesquiterpene]]s.
* α-[[Pinene]]<ref name=essential>{{cite journal |doi=10.1002/ffj.993 |title=Essential oils of different cultivars of ''Cannabis sativa'' L. and their antimicrobial activity |year=2001 |vauthors=Novak J, Zitterl-Eglseer K, Deans SG, Franz CM |journal=Flavour and Fragrance Journal |volume=16 |issue=4 |pages=259–262}}</ref>
* [[Myrcene]]<ref name=essential/>
* [[Linalool]]<ref name=essential/>
* [[Limonene]]<ref name=essential/>
* Trans-β-[[ocimene]]<ref name=essential/>
* α-[[Terpinolene]]<ref name=essential/>
* Trans-[[caryophyllene]]<ref name=essential/>
* α-[[Humulene]],<ref name=essential/> contributes to the characteristic aroma of ''Cannabis sativa''
* [[Caryophyllene]],<ref name=essential/> with which some hashish detection dogs are trained<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.bojensen.net/EssentialOilsEng/EssentialOils13A/EssentialOils13A.htm |title=Essential Oils |access-date=2007-10-11 |archive-date=2019-12-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191223140607/http://www.bojensen.net/EssentialOilsEng/EssentialOils13A/EssentialOils13A.htm |url-status=live }}</ref>

Cannabis also produces numerous volatile sulfur compounds that contribute to the plant's skunk-like aroma, with [[prenylthiol]] (3-methyl-2-butene-1-thiol) identified as the primary odorant.<ref>{{Cite journal|display-authors=3|last1=Oswald|first1=Iain W. H.|last2=Ojeda|first2=Marcos A.|last3=Pobanz|first3=Ryan J.|last4=Koby|first4=Kevin A.|last5=Buchanan|first5=Anthony J.|last6=Del Rosso|first6=Josh|last7=Guzman|first7=Mario A.|last8=Martin|first8=Thomas J.|date=2021-11-30|title=Identification of a New Family of Prenylated Volatile Sulfur Compounds in Cannabis Revealed by Comprehensive Two-Dimensional Gas Chromatography|url=https://doi.org/10.1021/acsomega.1c04196|journal=ACS Omega|volume=6|issue=47|pages=31667–31676|doi=10.1021/acsomega.1c04196|doi-access=free|pmid=34869990| issn=2470-1343|pmc=8638000}}</ref> These compounds are found in much lower concentrations than the major terpenes and sesquiterpenes. However, they contribute significantly to the pungent aroma of cannabis due to their [[Odor detection threshold|low odor thresholds]] as often seen with [[thiol]]s or other sulfur-containing compounds.

A number of specific aromatic compounds have been implicated in variety-specific aromas.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Oswald |first1=Iain W. H. |last2=Paryani |first2=Twinkle R. |last3=Sosa |first3=Manuel E. |last4=Ojeda |first4=Marcos A. |last5=Altenbernd |first5=Mark R. |last6=Grandy |first6=Jonathan J. |last7=Shafer |first7=Nathan S. |last8=Ngo |first8=Kim |last9=Peat |first9=Jack R. |last10=Melshenker |first10=Bradley G. |last11=Skelly |first11=Ian |last12=Koby |first12=Kevin A. |last13=Page |first13=Michael'' f. ''Z. |last14=Martin |first14=Thomas J. |date=2023-10-12 |title=Minor, Nonterpenoid Volatile Compounds Drive the Aroma Differences of Exotic Cannabis |journal=ACS Omega |volume=8 |issue=42 |pages=39203–39216 |language=en |doi=10.1021/acsomega.3c04496 |issn=2470-1343|doi-access=free |pmid=37901519 |pmc=10601067 }}</ref> These include another class of volatile sulfur compounds, referred to as tropical volatile sulfur compounds, that include 3-mercaptohexanol, 3-mercaptohexyl acetate, and 3-mercaptohexyl butyrate. These compounds possess powerful and distinctive fruity, tropical, and citrus aromas in low concentrations such as those found in certain cannabis varieties. These compounds are also important in the citrus and tropical flavors of [[hops]], [[beer]], [[wine]], and tropical fruits.

In addition to volatile sulfur compounds, the heterocyclic compounds [[indole]] and [[skatole]] (3-Methyl-1''H''-indole) contribute to the chemical or savory aromas of certain varieties.<ref name=":0" /> Skatole in particular was identified as a key contributor to this scent. This compound is found in mammalian feces and is used in the perfuming industry.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yokoyama |first1=Mt |last2=Carlson |first2=Jr |date=January 1979 |title=Microbial metabolites of tryptophan in the intestinal tract with special reference to skatole |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0002916523286852 |journal=The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition |language=en |volume=32 |issue=1 |pages=173–178 |doi=10.1093/ajcn/32.1.173|doi-access=free |pmid=367144 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> It possesses a complex aroma that is highly dependent on concentration.

==Cultivation==
A ''Cannabis'' plant in the vegetative growth phase requires more than 16–18 hours of light per day to stay vegetative. Flowering usually occurs when darkness equals at least 12 hours per day. The flowering cycle can last anywhere between seven and fifteen weeks, depending on the strain and environmental conditions. When the production of psychoactive [[cannabinoids]] is sought, female plants are grown separately from male plants to induce [[parthenocarpy]] in the female plant's fruits (popularly called {{lang|es|sin semilla}} which is [[Spanish language|Spanish]] for "without seed") and increase the production of [[cannabinoid]]-rich resin.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Riboulet-Zemouli K |title='Cannabis' Ontologies I: Conceptual Issues with Cannabis and Cannabinoids terminology |journal=Drug Science, Policy and Law |date=2020 |volume=6 |pages=1–37 |article-number=2050324520945797 |doi=10.1177/2050324520945797 |issn=2050-3245 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

In soil, the optimum [[pH]] for the plant is 6.3 to 6.8. In [[hydroponics|hydroponic]] growing, the nutrient solution is best at 5.2 to 5.8, making ''Cannabis'' well-suited to hydroponics because this pH range is hostile to most bacteria and fungi.{{fact|date=March 2026}}

[[Tissue culture]] multiplication has become important in producing medically important clones,<ref name="Arora2010">{{cite book |vauthors=Arora R |title=Medicinal Plant Biotechnology |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3sPwKo3b3cUC&pg=PA103 |year=2010 |publisher=CABI |isbn=978-1-84593-692-1 |pages=103ff |access-date=2018-02-27 |archive-date=2023-04-20 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230420161312/https://books.google.com/books?id=3sPwKo3b3cUC&pg=PA103 |url-status=live }}</ref> while seed production remains the generally preferred means of multiplication.<ref name="ChandraLata2017">{{cite book |vauthors=Chandra S, Lata H, El Sohly MA |title=Cannabis sativa L. – Botany and Biotechnology |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yfokDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA54 |date=23 May 2017 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-319-54564-6 |pages=54ff}}</ref> Sativa plants have narrow leaves and grow best in warm environments. They do, however, take longer to flower than their Indica counterparts, and they grow taller than the Indica cannabis strains as well.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Difference Between Indica and Sativa |url=https://maxindoorgrow.com/2019/12/12/the-similarities-and-difference-between-indica-and-sativa/ |date=2019-12-12 |website=Max's Indoor Grow Shop |language=en-US |access-date=2020-05-08 |archive-date=2020-07-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200727083314/https://maxindoorgrow.com/2019/12/12/the-similarities-and-difference-between-indica-and-sativa/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Cultivars ===
Broadly, there are three main [[cultivar|cultivar groups]] of cannabis that are cultivated today:
* Cultivars primarily cultivated for their fibre, characterized by long stems and little branching.<ref name="domestication">{{cite news |title=Cannabis first domesticated 12,000 years ago: study |url=https://phys.org/news/2021-07-cannabis-domesticated-years.html |access-date=18 July 2021 |work=Phys.org |date=17 July 2021 |language=en |archive-date=18 July 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210718024838/https://phys.org/news/2021-07-cannabis-domesticated-years.html |url-status=live }}</ref>
* Cultivars grown for seed which can be eaten entirely raw or from which [[hemp oil]] is extracted.
* Cultivars grown for medicinal or [[recreational drug use|recreational]] purposes, characterized by extensive branching to maximize the number of flowers.<ref name="domestication"/>
[[File:Annibale Genetics strain example.jpg|thumb|Genetic traits in a Sativa Cannabis plant well grown<ref>{{Cite book |last=Green |first=Greg |title=The Cannabis Grow Bible vol.4 |publisher=GREEN CANDY PRESS |year=2025 |isbn=9781937866785 |edition=4th}}</ref>]]
A nominal if not legal distinction is often made between industrial hemp, with concentrations of psychoactive compounds far too low to be useful for that purpose, and [[Marijuana (word)|marijuana]].

== Uses ==
{{Main|Cannabis#Industrial and personal uses|l1 = Industrial and personal uses of ''cannabis''|Cannabis (drug)|Hemp}}

''Cannabis sativa'' seeds are chiefly used to make hempseed oil which can be used for cooking, lamps, lacquers, or paints. They can also be used as caged-bird feed, as they provide a source of nutrients for most animals. The flowers and fruits (and to a lesser extent the leaves, stems, and seeds) contain [[psychoactive]] [[chemical compound]]s known as [[cannabinoids]] that are consumed for recreational, medicinal, and spiritual purposes. When so used, preparations of flowers and fruits (called [[marijuana]]) and leaves and preparations derived from resinous extract (e.g., [[hashish]]) are consumed by smoking, vaporising, and oral ingestion. Historically, [[tincture]]s, [[Herbal tea|teas]], and [[ointment]]s have also been common preparations. In [[traditional medicine]] of India in particular ''cannabis sativa'' has been used as hallucinogenic, hypnotic, [[sedative]], [[analgesic]], and [[anti-inflammatory]] agent.<ref name="pmid30205181">{{cite journal |vauthors=Bonini SA, Premoli M, Tambaro S, Kumar A, Maccarinelli G, Memo M, Mastinu A |date=December 2018 |title=Cannabis sativa: A comprehensive ethnopharmacological review of a medicinal plant with a long history |journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology |volume=227 |issue= |pages=300–315 |doi=10.1016/j.jep.2018.09.004 |pmid=30205181 |s2cid=52188193}}</ref> Terpenes have gained public awareness through the growth and education of medical and recreational cannabis. Organizations and companies operating in cannabis markets have pushed education and marketing of terpenes in their products as a way to differentiate taste and effects of cannabis.<ref>{{cite web |title=Terpene Carene usage |url=https://terpenoids.net/terpene-carene/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200809004529/https://terpenoids.net/terpene-carene/|url-status=dead|archive-date=August 9, 2020}}</ref> The [[entourage effect]], which describes the synergy of cannabinoids, terpenes, and other plant compounds, has also helped further awareness and demand for terpenes in cannabis products.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Goldstein Ferber |first=Sari |date=February 18, 2020 |title=The "Entourage Effect": Terpenes Coupled with Cannabinoids for the Treatment of Mood Disorders and Anxiety Disorders |journal=Current Neuropharmacology |volume=18 |issue=2 |pages=87–96 |doi=10.2174/1570159X17666190903103923 |pmc=7324885 |pmid=31481004}}</ref>
